title: Pterygium excision with conjunctival autograft
subtitle: Excision, bare sclera bed and a limbal-oriented conjunctival graft

sources.org: Clearfield E et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev (CD011349)
sources.title: Conjunctival autograft for pterygium

indications: Pterygium encroaching on the visual axis or progressing towards it.
Astigmatism induced by the pterygium, restriction of eye movement, persistent irritation, or cosmetic concern after discussion.
Doubt about the diagnosis (ocular surface squamous neoplasia can mimic pterygium): excision for histology.
contraindications: Active ocular surface inflammation until controlled.
preparation: Measure the extent onto the cornea and the induced astigmatism; photograph.
Consent: recurrence (much lower with a graft than bare sclera), graft retraction or loss, scarring, double vision from muscle restriction, dellen, and need for further surgery.
positioning: Supine with the head flat and level, chin and forehead in one horizontal plane, a head ring or gel pillow; the head of the patient at the end of the table so the surgeon can sit.
equipment: Blade or crescent blade, Westcott or Vannas scissors, non-toothed forceps, diamond burr or blade for corneal polishing, wet-field cautery, fibrin glue or 8-0 absorbable and 10-0 nylon sutures, calipers.
anatomy: The pterygium head on the cornea, its body on the nasal (usually) bulbar conjunctiva, the underlying Tenon's and the medial rectus a few millimetres behind the limbus.
The superior bulbar conjunctiva is the donor site: thin, with its own limbal border.
criticalSafety: Do not damage the medial rectus when removing Tenon's.
Orient the graft limbus to limbus.
Send the tissue for histology when the appearance is atypical.
commonErrors: A thick graft with Tenon's on it.
complications: Diplopia from muscle injury or scarring.
postop: Steroid and antibiotic drops on a taper; pad overnight.
Review at one day and one week to check the graft; recurrence check over the following year.

steps.emphasis: Mark the eye and the side of the pterygium (nasal or temporal).
Topical drops with subconjunctival local anaesthetic under the pterygium is usual.
Supine with the head flat and level, chin and forehead in one horizontal plane, a head ring or gel pillow; the head of the patient at the end of the table so the surgeon can sit.
Light wet-field cautery only to the bleeding points; heavy cautery thins sclera.
Send the pterygium for histology; label atypical features.

step.ptg.excise.title: Excising the pterygium head and body
step.ptg.excise.why: The head comes off the cornea and the body with its fibrovascular Tenon's is removed. Leaving the abnormal Tenon's drives recurrence; cutting too deep injures the medial rectus.
how: Separate the head from the cornea by blunt avulsion or careful dissection in the plane above Bowman's layer.
Excise the conjunctival body and dissect the abnormal subconjunctival Tenon's off the sclera, staying anterior to the muscle insertion.
Leave a bare scleral bed of known size; measure it with calipers.
pitfalls: Leaving thick Tenon's on the bed.

step.ptg.cornea.title: Smoothing the cornea
step.ptg.cornea.why: Residual tissue on the cornea gives an irregular surface and invites recurrence.
how: Remove residual fibrovascular tissue from the cornea with a blade or diamond burr.
Keep the keratectomy superficial and smooth.

step.ptg.graft-harvest.title: Harvesting the conjunctival autograft
step.ptg.graft-harvest.why: A thin, Tenon-free graft with its limbal edge marked is what lowers the recurrence rate. A thick graft retracts and a misoriented one fails.
how: Measure the bed and mark a graft about 0.5 to 1 mm larger at the superior bulbar conjunctiva.
Balloon the conjunctiva with saline or local anaesthetic, and dissect a thin graft free of Tenon's up to the limbus.
Mark the limbal edge so it is not inverted or rotated.
pitfalls: Losing track of the limbal edge.

step.ptg.graft-secure.title: Securing the graft limbus to limbus
step.ptg.graft-secure.why: The limbal edge of the graft carries stem cells that act as a barrier; facing the cornea, it reduces recurrence.
how: Slide the graft onto the bed with its limbal edge at the limbus, epithelial side up.
Secure with fibrin glue or interrupted absorbable sutures, smoothing out folds and expressing any blood under it.
Close or leave the donor site per technique.
pitfalls: Blood or folds under the graft.

step.ptg.bailout.title: Bailout: scleral thinning, muscle exposure or an atypical lesion
step.ptg.bailout.why: Unexpected findings change the operation: thin sclera may need a patch, a damaged muscle needs repair, and a lesion that looks like neoplasia needs a different, no-touch excision with margins.
how: If the medial rectus is exposed or cut, identify the ends and repair with absorbable suture, or call a strabismus surgeon.
If the sclera is very thin, avoid further cautery and cover it (graft or patch).
If the lesion looks like ocular surface squamous neoplasia (gelatinous, leukoplakic, unusual vessels), excise with margins and cryotherapy per protocol, or stop after biopsy and refer.
pitfalls: Treating a neoplastic lesion as a simple pterygium.
